title: Imam al-Maturidi
hook: a theologian in Samarqand, close to the Ash'aris, with one difference worth knowing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ash'ari school, and your line: the middle way. Did you find one thing each side got right? Today, a second Sunni school, from far to the east. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.

Basra and Baghdad have been the stage all week. Now go east, past Iran, across the great river, into what is now Uzbekistan. Samarqand: a city of traders and scholars on the Silk Road. A theologian named Abu Mansur al-Maturidi taught there; his name, the sources say, comes from Maturid, a quarter of the city. He was a Hanafi, trained in the legal school of Abu Hanifa, and he wrote a book called simply Kitab al-Tawhid, the book of oneness. He was working on the same questions as al-Ash'ari, far from Basra, and reaching answers that sit very close. Today, the man from Samarqand.

Start with how close the two schools are. Ash'aris and Maturidis both defend traditional Sunni belief with reason. Both say the Qur'an is Allah's uncreated speech. Both affirm His attributes. Later scholars often named them together as the two Sunni schools of kalam, and the Maturidi school became tied especially with Hanafi scholars. Now the one difference worth learning. Can a person know, by reason alone, that some things are good and some are bad, before any messenger arrives? The Ash'aris said our obligations come from revelation. Without a messenger, no duty is laid on us. Al-Maturidi gave reason a bigger job. Reason, in his view, can recognize that lying is ugly and that gratitude is right, and can even grasp that the world has a Maker who deserves thanks. Revelation confirms and fills in what reason sees. It doesn't contradict it. Both schools agree that Allah is just and that the Qur'an guides. They disagree about how much the mind can see on its own. That's a fair disagreement, and Sunni scholars kept both schools in their curricula. And that rounds off a week. We began with faith that rises and falls, then kalam, speaking about Allah with arguments. Then the Mu'tazilah and their justice, the trial and Ahmad ibn Hanbal's refusal, al-Ash'ari's turn, his school's middle way, and now Samarqand. One conversation, carried from city to city.
screen: `TWO SCHOOLS, VERY CLOSE.` · `CAN REASON KNOW GOOD AND BAD?` · `AL-MATURIDI: IT CAN SEE SOME.` · then, large: `ONE CONVERSATION, CITY TO CITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one difference. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you know is good without having to look it up: thanking someone who helped you, or telling the truth when a lie would be easier. Ask yourself the Samarqand question: how do I know this is good? From a text, from a parent, from something in me that recognizes it? There's no test here. Just notice where the knowing seems to come from. If you pray, you can give thanks for whatever showed it to you. The bell holds the time.
Imam al-Maturidi. The Hanafi theologian of Samarqand, close to the Ash'aris, who gave reason a larger role in knowing good and bad. Today's word.
Your line: from samarqand. Today, when you do something good, ask once how you knew it was good. Tomorrow, the Athari approach. Day one thousand two hundred forty-six.
